title: The tithe (Malachi 3:10)
hookLine: many Christians give a tenth; others give differently, but most give regularly

cards: Payday. The money lands in your account, and within minutes it's already spoken for: rent, groceries, the phone bill, the car, the thing you promised your kid. Whatever's left at the end of the month is what's left.

Now go back to Genesis, to Abram, the man who'll become Abraham. He's just come back from a battle, and a mysterious priest-king named Melchizedek comes out to meet him with bread and wine, and blesses him.
Abram's response fits in one line. In the King James words: "And he gave him tithes of all." A tenth of everything.

teach.b: Tithe is an old English word meaning a tenth.
In the Hebrew scriptures, tithes of grain, wine, oil and flocks supported the priests and Levites who served at the sanctuary, and some went to the poor: the widow, the orphan and the stranger.

Then the prophet Malachi, speaking to people who had held back their tithes: "Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the LORD of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing."
Christians today read that verse in different ways. Some churches, often evangelical or Pentecostal, teach tithing as a standard: a tenth of income, given to the local church.

teach.h: A TENTH, OR A CHEERFUL GIVER.
teach.b: Others, Catholic and Orthodox among them, teach generous, regular giving without a fixed number, and point to Paul: "every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
Some preachers read Malachi as a promise that giving will make you rich; other Christians firmly reject that reading.
A thread through these views is firstfruits. Proverbs says, "Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase." The first of the harvest, not the leftovers.
For those who teach it, the point isn't the math. It's the order. Giving that comes first shapes everything after it.
Giving that waits for the leftovers often finds none.

how: Christians give to their church and to the poor in different ways; some tithe ten percent of their income, while others give a proportion they decide themselves, often through a weekly offering or a regular automatic gift.

games.q: it's payday. rent, groceries, bills. you want to give something regularly. when do you set the gift aside?
games.why: the old word is firstfruits: honor God with the first of the harvest. giving first shapes everything after it.

practice: Think of something you care about, a church, a food bank, a neighbor, a cause, and one small, regular gift you could give it: money in an amount so small it doesn't scare you, an hour a month, or a skill.
Don't decide the whole plan, only the first gift and when it happens. If you pray, offer it to God before it leaves your hands; if you don't, simply choose it freely.

wordCard.voice: Tithe. A tenth: the old practice of giving the first part of what you have to God and to those in need. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a tenth, a tithe. from eser, ten.

carryVoice: Your line: give first, not last. The gift itself can be small. That's day one hundred thirty-one.
